claims.text:
self-play

**Identity / target / source:** `ai:self-play` → `ai-self-play` → `src/demos/ai/ai-self-play`; source `company/domains/proposals/2026-10-18-ai-map-expansion.json#concepts/111`; brief `company/domains/briefs/2026-10-19-ai-next30e.md#11-self-play`. **Packet:** R2. **Level / prerequisites:** core; `ai:policy-gradient`.

**Nearest / distinct payoff:** policy-gradient reinforces sampled actions; this computes best-response policy replacement against a changing opponent and tests population strength.

**Computed primary model:** Rock-paper-scissors payoff matrix row player: tie0, win+1, loss−1. Opponent starts Rock. Policy update selects a pure best response: Paper wins+1 against Rock. Replace opponent with latest policyPaper; next best responseScissors wins+1; thenRock wins+1 againstScissors. Relative success improves against each last opponent while the policies cycle.

**Countercase / boundary:** Test each new pure policy against uniform opponent[1/3,1/3,1/3]: expected payoff0 throughout. TestPaper againstScissors and it loses−1 despite beating the oldRock. A uniform opponent population has tied best responses; use stable Rock tie rule rather than inventing increasing strength.

**Prediction / transfer recall:** Predict next best response after opponentPaper; recall why winning against the last opponent alone does not imply monotonically greater general ability.

**Intervention / retained witness:** Update opponent/Best respond computes the matrix row, current opponent payoff and uniform-population payoff; retain the fullR→P→S→R cycle. This is exact best-response replacement, not an implemented policy-gradient training loop.
